cases.title: Finca 470: an IDB road loan's forest offset and the Ache Kuetuvy's land title
cases.place: Finca 470, next to the Mbaracayu Forest Nature Reserve, Canindeyu department, Paraguay
cases.point: Mbaracayu Forest Nature Reserve (coordinates from the Wikipedia article on the reserve, which gives 24.122114 S, 55.447028 W). Finca 470 is contiguous to the reserve; the MICI report gives no coordinates and its own boundary was not found. Sources place it in different districts, including inside the MICI report itself: paragraph 3.41 says the District of Curuguaty, while the report's own description of the request says the Ache community of the Ygatimi District. The report adds that Finca 470 is about 50 kilometres from Curuguaty.

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
lenders.role: Loan 933/OC-PR, Program to Improve Highway Corridors in Paraguay (PR-0035). The MICI report says the Loan Contract was approved in 1996 and records design and approval in the period 1993 to 1996 and first disbursement in February 1998. The report gives two dates for the last disbursement and does not settle between them in its own text: 31 August 2009, per the Project Completion Report, and 30 December 2007. At a meeting on 1 May 2012 Management told the Panel the Project Completion Report date was wrong and that 30 December 2007 was correct. Management's explanation is that the Project Completion Report 'contained an involuntary error' when it gave August 2009 and that all other IDB systems record the 2007 date. Management used the 2007 date to argue the request should have been declared ineligible, because the ICIM Policy bars requests filed more than 24 months after the last disbursement and the request was filed in November 2010, 35 months later. The Panel took the case forward. Bank policy at the time did not allow land to be bought with loan proceeds, so the offset land was to be bought with Paraguay's own counterpart funds: US$4 million for forest reserves and US$2 million for indigenous lands.

cases.conditions: The loan's Environmental Sub-Program required Paraguay to buy 20,000 hectares for forest reserves and 11,000 hectares to regularise indigenous land ownership, as an offset for what the report calls the likely ecological and social impacts of future road works. Management says the loan contract was negotiated on a fixed dollar amount for land, on the assumption that US$4 million and US$2 million would buy those areas; the Panel says the basis for those calculations does not appear to have been clear, and that both allocations proved insufficient. The December 1995 Environmental Summary had set out conditions to be met before loan approval and before first disbursement, including a land-titling plan naming the indigenous communities to benefit, the hectares and funding for each, and a timetable for acquisition and demarcation. The MICI panel found this phased approach was never written into the loan contract and never put into effect.
cases.community: The MICI panel says Finca 470 covers approximately 4,760 hectares (paragraph 3.41); Management's response gives 4,600 hectares. The Moises Bertoni Foundation was finalising a purchase of it from its Taiwanese owner, who also owned a nearby sawmill, in order to transfer ownership to the Ache Kuetuvy, who had been settled on the property since 2000. The Panel records that by the time the Ministry of Public Works and Communications began buying land to meet the loan's requirements, the Foundation was already finalising negotiations, having sent representatives to Taiwan twice and enlisted Paraguay's ambassador there. The Panel then says: 'Once the Taiwanese owner learned about the MOPC's interest in purchasing Finca 470, he abandoned the close to final negotiations with FMB.' The ministry bought Finca 470 in 2003 for slightly more than the value set by a 2002 valuation the IDB had commissioned, and transferred the title to the environment ministry SEAM. The Panel notes the IDB had been concerned about a possible large disparity between what the Foundation would have had to pay and the price the ministry would pay; the report does not say what the Foundation's price was, and does not state that the ministry outbid it. People the Panel interviewed in Paraguay said the ministry's purchase and the transfer to SEAM prevented the Foundation's purchase and the promised transfer to the Ache Kuetuvy. SEAM ceded temporary usufruct to the indigenous institute INDI in 2004 so the Ache could continue their way of life, as a first step towards legal transfer. A letter of November 2005 from the then SEAM minister to the Ache leader Margarita Mbywangi said the community was authorised to patrol and control Finca 470 and that the transfer process was at an advanced stage. The Ache developed and ran a certified forest management plan, funded by Conservation International, and IDB funds paid a Paraguayan lawyer to advance the titling. After elections in 2008 and a new administration at SEAM the earlier agreements were suspended, and on 21 June 2010 SEAM enacted Resolution 662/10, seeking to divide Finca 470 between the Ache Kuetuvy and the Ava Guarani communities of Ytu and Ka'a Poty. SEAM told the Panel its new senior staff believed the area was part of both peoples' ancestral territory. The Ava Guarani on the edge of the finca are described in the report as families living as campesinos in extreme poverty who urgently need access to land. The report records 4 or 5 Ava families on the edge of the property when the Ache returned in 2000, and a recent influx of more.
cases.suppression: The report records that in 2006 several Ache were imprisoned for defending the land. Paragraph 3.45 says the IDB agreed to use project funds for a lawyer to obtain the release from prison of several Ache leaders who had been imprisoned in 2006 after they resisted an invasion of loggers into Finca 470; the invaders claimed title to an area labelled Finca 27 which in their view partly overlapped Finca 470. In his letter transmitting the report on 20 November 2012, the Panel chair wrote that 'reports from Paraguay indicate that starting in May 2012 and until today, a group of heavily armed illegal loggers has invaded Finca 470', that the group 'is threatening violence against the Ache' and is 'cutting down large trees in Finca 470 sold as illegal timber'. That is the Panel relaying reports, not a finding of its own. Global Voices, citing ABC Color, reports that peasant groups issued death threats to Ache who tried to stop the logging and to journalists covering it, and that on 15 August 2012 at 19:30 the community leader Margarita Mbywangi took a call from a man identifying himself as a peasant who said that if young Ache hunters came near them they would be killed. The people making these threats were invaders and loggers, not the lender or a project contractor.
cases.killed_note: The Requesters told MICI that in the spring of 1992 the Ache were expelled from the area that now includes Finca 470 and forcibly moved to a reservation 100 km to the south-west, and that an estimated 40 per cent of the community died as a result, which led to international allegations of genocide. This was before the IDB loan and is not counted here. Reported by the Requesters in the panel report, not a panel finding.
cases.ecosystem: The panel's conclusion at paragraph 5.2 is that the implementation of the environmental component of the project must be judged to have failed, that the hectare targets were not reached, and that, aside from a few exceptions, notably Finca 470, 'it appears that much of the forest land, that should have been protected in perpetuity has been unsustainably logged or completely cleared'. The hedge 'it appears that' is the panel's own wording. At paragraph 4.38 the panel says it 'was alerted to the deforestation of an area of 1,600 ha. that had been purchased by MOPC for conservation'. Management's own account says those 1,600 hectares were still under negotiation and that the ministry was about to buy them; no source explains the gap between the two accounts. A panel annex says land bought by Paraguay to meet the IDB offset targets had already been largely deforested, and suggests giving it to the Ava Guarani because it would suit their farming. At paragraph 5.12 the panel says it was informed that Law 4304/11 transferred Finca 470 to the Ache but that the land had not yet been officially transferred, 'prompting illegal logging and invasions by unauthorized people'. At paragraph 2.32 the panel says recent increases in attempts to carry out more illegal logging in Finca 470 have been observed, as Ava Guarani on the edge of the finca and others seek to earn a living from logging the forest. The report says the region had lost an estimated 87 per cent of its forest ecosystem by the 1990s, and that only the Mbaracayu Natural Reserve, which it gives as 64,400 hectares, and Finca 470 next to it remain in a largely pristine condition; the two are described as an 'island of trees in a sea of agro-business expansion'. The report gives two figures for what is left of the Atlantic Forest: paragraph 2.34 says 99,944 of an original 1,233,875 square kilometres remain, which it puts at 7 per cent, while paragraph 3.41 says the forest type at Finca 470 has been reduced to less than 5 per cent of its original range.
cases.outcome: The panel found the IDB failed to enforce compliance with the Environment Policy (OP-703), Project Preparation, Evaluation and Approval (OP-302) and Operations Administration (OP-304). It said the project interfered with an almost completed purchase of Finca 470 on behalf of the Ache, and that the later shortage of properly managed social offset land led SEAM to propose giving a large part of the promised land to an Ava Guarani group that had not helped manage it or submitted a management plan. It also found an apparent lack of systematic monitoring of the offset purchases and of titling to indigenous communities. Portfolio reviews in 2004 and 2005 found the consolidated land-purchase plan only partly implemented and the loan clauses on land for protected areas and indigenous peoples in full or partial non-compliance. In the letter transmitting the report on 20 November 2012, the panel chair wrote that after the draft report was circulated on 21 February 2012 the panel received information that on 26 July 2012 the Government of Paraguay granted the Ache Kuetuvy community legal title to Finca 470, and that the problem at the centre of the request 'appears to be solved'.

cases.confidence_note: IDB Management told the panel that loan 933/OC-PR financed no upgrading or paving work on Route 10, only work on Route 3, so the Ache sit in the indirect area of influence of a road the Bank never financed; on that basis Management called the harm argument irrelevant and outside MICI's remit, and said the Ache had usufruct, which it considered a legally viable way of meeting the project's objective. Management also argued the request should have been ruled ineligible as filed 35 months after the last disbursement. The panel found non-compliance anyway. The panel's wording about harm is not consistent, and all three forms are printed here rather than reconciled: paragraph 4.15 calls the failure to enforce compliance 'an important cause for the harm alleged by the Ache'; paragraph 4.16 calls the non-adherence to the offset provisions and the resulting shortage of land 'an important cause for the harm now experienced by the Ache'; and the executive summary says that breaking the promise of title 'threatens to bring direct material harm to them as a community and as individuals'. What the report records as having happened is the abandoned Foundation purchase, roughly ten years in which the Ache occupied Finca 470 without title until 26 July 2012, the imprisonment of several Ache leaders in 2006 after they resisted a logger invasion, and logging or clearing on offset land and on Finca 470. The 1992 expulsion and death toll are the Requesters' account, not a finding. The death threats of 2012 come from Global Voices citing ABC Color. The ABC Color article was listed as a source by the writer of the draft and was not opened during this check, so no figure here rests on it alone.
cx: Program to Improve Highway Corridors in Paraguay

lvwhy.land: The loan required Paraguay to buy 20,000 ha of forest reserve and 11,000 ha for indigenous communities as an offset; the ministry's purchase of Finca 470 under that requirement is what the panel says interfered with the sale that would have titled the land to the Ache.
lvwhy.project: The money was a road programme loan, and the offset land purchases were a condition of it.

cases.whole: Management says Paraguay spent US$4,411,794 on 8,365 hectares of uncultivated land, including 1,600 hectares under negotiation, and US$2,375,000 on 10,975 hectares for indigenous communities, of which 1,000 hectares were bought with local funds through INDI and 4,600 hectares were Finca 470, first bought as an environmental protection area. Elsewhere in the same response Management says two lots totalling 6,765 hectares were bought for woodland conservation and that an estimated 9,375 hectares in all went to seven indigenous communities, with a further 1,600 hectares about to be bought. The committed targets were 20,000 and 11,000 hectares. Management explains the shortfall by delays pushing up land prices between design in 1993-96 and the last disbursement; the panel says the planned upgrading of Highway 10 most certainly led to land speculation in the region and possibly inflated prices, and that the offset strategy lacked realism about land availability and counterpart funds from the start. Separately, the panel records that The Nature Conservancy and the Moises Bertoni Foundation bought the Mbaracayu Forest from the International Finance Corporation for US$2 million in 1991, after the IFC took the land as collateral when a Paraguayan timber company defaulted on an IFC loan, with USAID, the energy company AES and other donors contributing; among the conditions of that sale was that the Ache's claims to continued use of the land be respected.

cases.title: Polihali Dam, Lesotho Highlands Phase II: cracked houses, relocations and falling land rates
cases.place: Polihali Dam and surrounding villages, Mokhotlong district, Lesotho
cases.point: Polihali dam site, which the AfDB's environmental and social impact assessment summary places downstream of the confluence of the Senqu and Khubelu rivers in Mokhotlong district. The point is approximate and the affected villages lie around the reservoir and along the access roads and transfer tunnel.

lenders.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
lenders.role: The AfDB's own appraisal report recommends, and its recommendation section states, a loan of one billion three hundred million South African rand (ZAR 1,300,000,000) to South Africa's Trans-Caledon Tunnel Authority, guaranteed by the Government of the Republic of South Africa. The report's currency equivalences are dated May 2021. Early Warning System, drawing on AfDB data, gives a board voting date of 6 October 2021, an investment amount of US$89.56 million and an AfDB figure of 62,683,227.9 units of account. A figure of US$86.72 million appears in the headlines of several news reports of the approval; none of those pages opened during this check, so that figure is not carried here. The AfDB loan and the NDB loan finance, on a pari passu basis, part of Component B, the main works covering the Polihali dam and the Polihali transfer tunnel.

lenders.name: New Development Bank (NDB)
lenders.role: Co-financier. The AfDB appraisal report says the NDB loan is ZAR 3.2 billion and was approved in March 2020. Accountability Counsel lists the NDB alongside the AfDB, the Development Bank of Southern Africa and the TCTA as co-financiers.

lenders.name: Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA)
lenders.role: Named as a co-financier by Accountability Counsel. The AfDB appraisal report does not name the DBSA; it says the Government of South Africa will provide the remaining 86.2 per cent of total project cost and that the TCTA will raise those funds from other banks and local bond issues. No DBSA loan figure is carried here, because the news report that gave one did not open during this check.

cases.conditions: Not extracted. The AfDB's appraisal report lists conditions tied to compensation and resettlement, including that funds for compensation or resettlement of project-affected persons be deposited in a special account and that affected people be compensated or resettled in line with the environmental and social management plan and the resettlement action plan. The terms were not read in full for this entry.

companies.name: Lesotho Highlands Development Authority (LHDA)
companies.role: Implementing authority inside Lesotho; runs the compensation and resettlement programme and is the respondent in the Lesotho High Court case and the subject of the AfDB complaint and the Ombudsman investigation
companies.desc: The Lesotho body that implements the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, established under the LHDA Order of 1986. Its spokesperson, quoted by GroundUp, is Mpho Brown.

companies.name: Trans-Caledon Tunnel Authority (TCTA)
companies.role: South African state-owned authority and the borrower of the AfDB loan
companies.desc: A South African state-owned entity that raises finance for and manages bulk water transfer infrastructure. The AfDB appraisal report names the TCTA as the borrower, with a guarantee from the Government of South Africa.

cases.community: Thirty-seven human rights defenders filed a complaint with the AfDB's accountability mechanism dated 11 September 2025, on behalf of 18 village communities of approximately 1,600 people, supported by the Seinoli Legal Centre and Accountability Counsel. The complaint names the communities as Ha-Phohla, Ha-Tlhakola, Ha-Konki, Namoha, Malubalube, Ha-Ramonakalali, Masakong, Tloha-re-Buoe, Kanana Mabothong, Kanana Khatleli, Lilimala, Tsekong, Makalong, Bokone, Makhoaba, Morojeleng, Ha-Ramoruti and Litsotsong, and describes them as primarily rural, pastoralist and farming communities. The documents address the mechanism as the Independent Recourse Mechanism (IRM); the AfDB's own reports from 2011 and 2022 call the same body the Independent Review Mechanism. The AfDB's appraisal report says the project requires the acquisition of about 5,600 hectares up to 2,080 metres above sea level, across four community councils (Seate, Bokong, Malingoaneng and Mphokojoane) and the Mokhotlong urban council; that about 2,300 households will be affected by Phase II, 69.6 per cent of them by the creation or filling of the reservoir; that approximately 342 households will have to be relocated, 96.2 per cent of them from the reservoir area and construction sites; and that total compensation is estimated at 980,375,887.56 maloti. The complainants say households in Tsekong, Ha-Konki and Litsotsong sit inside the dam construction perimeter and were to have been relocated before works began but are still there; that blasting and tunnel boring have cracked houses in Tsekong, Ha-Konki, Sekokong, Tloha-re-Buoe, Kanana-Mabothong and Makhoaba; that rocks were thrown into yards and homes during blasting and excavation; and that LHDA's consultant SUN JV has denied responsibility for the quarry blasting damage. They also say grazing land has been fenced, access to forest for firewood and medicinal plants lost, traditional paths blocked, harvests reduced, that women are excluded from compensation and decision-making, and that an influx of male workers has raised safety and health concerns. GroundUp reports residents in Tsekong, Ha Konki and Sekokong saying vibrations have left homes cracked and unsafe and some now uninhabitable. The Ombudsman's report records that some residents reported unfinished resettlement houses lacking promised social infrastructure such as water, electricity and access roads. In a separate constitutional case in the Lesotho High Court, more than 3,000 individuals and 889 registered businesses are suing the LHDA and its contractors; the lead applicant is the Mokhotlong Business Forum Development Trust, whose chairperson Limpho Natsoane says in a founding affidavit that the LHDA failed in its constitutional duty to compensate promptly and fully. The applicants say losses dating back to 1987 include communal grazing land, medicinal plants, wild vegetables, brushwood and grasses, that their cattle are dying for lack of pastureland, that land was expropriated for over 37 years without fair compensation, and that a promised community development fund was never set up.
cases.suppression: Complainants allege harassment or arrest when they protest or demand accountability. The High Court applicants ask the court to declare that the arrest, detention, torture and prosecution of some individuals, allegedly by police acting with LHDA agents, were unconstitutional. Seinoli alleges some people were made to sign compensation agreements under threat of expropriation without compensation. These are the complainants' and applicants' allegations; no finding on them was found in the documents opened for this check.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the documents read.
cases.displaced_note: No figure for households actually moved was found in any page opened for this check. The AfDB's appraisal report of 2021 is a forward-looking plan: about 2,300 households affected and approximately 342 to be relocated. Accountability Counsel said on 17 February 2026 that relocation remains incomplete, and the Lesotho Ombudsman in June 2026 ordered three villages relocated within six months. A news report carrying the LHDA's own count of households relocated by April 2025 did not open during this check, so no number is given here.
cases.ecosystem: The AfDB appraisal report says the project requires acquiring about 5,600 hectares up to 2,080 metres above sea level, and that the aim is to raise the transfer of water from Lesotho to South Africa from 780 million cubic metres a year to 1,260 million. Complainants say blasting raises heavy dust with a strong chemical smell and contaminates nearby water sources, so that women walk long distances when sources are polluted or pipes are damaged, and that grazing land has been fenced and forest access lost. Public Eye reports that the LHDA noted some villagers said dust was manageable, and that the Ombudsman concluded mitigation measures are grossly inadequate and recommended professional-grade sound barriers along residential borders and regulated periodic watering to suppress dust.
cases.outcome: In June 2026 the Lesotho Ombudsman, Advocate Tlotliso Polaki, released a report on the project and presented it at a press briefing in Maseru. Public Eye quotes the report as saying 'Reports indicated indiscriminate blasting negatively impacting resident safety and causing property damage', and reports that during site inspections the Ombudsman's investigators documented several houses with severe structural cracks and, in at least one case, a complete house collapse. Public Eye does not say which villages those houses were in. The Ombudsman ordered the LHDA, within six months, to relocate the three villages of Masakong, Tlhakola and Tsekong 'to avoid unnecessary casualties given the current state of houses and proximity to construction activities', to provide direct financial redress to all affected households including those with outstanding claims dating back to 2012, to rectify all unfinished houses and provide the promised social infrastructure, and to put in place interim livelihood support for families whose incomes have been suspended. Public Eye reports that the LHDA submitted data on 19 March, with no year given in the article, saying 48 damaged houses had been repaired, 24 under the dam project and 20 under the tunnel project, and that the Ombudsman found the pace of repairs dangerously slow and that many families continue to live in compromised dwellings. The two component figures add to 44, not 48; no source explains that gap, and the arithmetic note is this check's, not Public Eye's. On compensation, Public Eye reports Phase I arrears of M142.2 million as at 31 December 2025 with future costs projected at M473 million, and Phase II arrears of M6.76 million with future costs near M25 million. It says the rate for expropriated land was initially set at M23 per square metre and that communities now report it has changed to as little as M0.98 per square metre in some areas and M0.68 in others, with no clear explanation from the LHDA; the reduced rates are what communities report, not an Ombudsman finding. GroundUp reports residents in Kanana-Mabothong and Popa saying the rate dropped from R23 per square metre in 2023 to 98 cents in 2024. The AfDB's mechanism registered the complaint; as of 17 February 2026 Accountability Counsel said AfDB Management had not yet clearly indicated whether it would engage in mediation, and that blasting continues and relocation remains incomplete. Seinoli and Accountability Counsel wrote to NDB president Dilma Rousseff and the NDB board on 19 June 2026 saying repeated engagement since August 2024 had produced no meaningful response, and said on 21 September 2026 that more than two months later the NDB had still not responded.

cases.confidence_note: The house damage is a finding of the Lesotho Ombudsman, a state office acting under a constitutional mandate to investigate maladministration and human rights violations by government agencies, reported by Public Eye: during site inspections her investigators documented several houses with severe structural cracks and in at least one case a complete house collapse. The Ombudsman tied the condition of houses to the project in ordering three villages relocated within six months to avoid unnecessary casualties given the current state of houses and their proximity to construction activities. The wording on cause is weaker than the wording on damage: the report as quoted says 'Reports indicated indiscriminate blasting negatively impacting resident safety and causing property damage', which is the Ombudsman relaying reports, while the cracks and the collapse were observed by her own investigators. Public Eye does not name the villages where the damaged houses were; the villages named for house damage in the complaint are Tsekong, Ha-Konki, Sekokong, Tloha-re-Buoe, Kanana-Mabothong and Makhoaba, and GroundUp names Tsekong, Ha Konki and Sekokong. The LHDA disputes the broader account. Its spokesperson Mpho Brown told GroundUp its operations are transparent and consultative, that it runs baseline property surveys within a kilometre of blasting sites, that no homes have been declared uninhabitable and fresh inspections are under way, that as of September 2025 more than R154 million had been paid for private assets with 93 per cent of acquired assets compensated, and that delays are mostly due to missing documents or family disputes. Both are printed: the Ombudsman records a collapsed house in June 2026; the LHDA said in 2025 that no homes had been declared uninhabitable. The LHDA does admit that a small number of vehicles encroached on fields and damaged crops, and says verified claims were compensated. The dust, water contamination, intimidation and gender claims rest on the complainants' accounts and are reported here as such. This is Phase II at Polihali in Mokhotlong, a different dam, different phase, different lenders and different villages from the Phase 1 case at Katse already on the map.
cx: Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II (Polihali Dam)

lvwhy.land: About 5,600 hectares are to be acquired for the reservoir and works, and the rate paid per square metre is reported to have fallen sharply between 2023 and 2024.
lvwhy.project: The AfDB and NDB loans finance the main works, the Polihali dam and the 38 km transfer tunnel, and the blasting and construction the damage follows.

cases.whole: The AfDB appraisal report puts the total project cost at ZAR 32.562 billion (1.576 billion units of account), net of taxes and duties, and says the Government of South Africa will provide the remaining 86.2 per cent of it. Phase II centres on the Polihali Dam in Mokhotlong district and a 38 km gravity tunnel linking the new Polihali reservoir to the existing Katse reservoir, plus major bridges on the A1 road and associated road works. The scheme is to raise Lesotho's hydropower capacity and increase water exports to South Africa's Vaal River system. The High Court applicants say Phase II construction began in March 2015 but the approved scheme was published only later that year, and that the LHDA proceeded without fully complying with compensation protocols and legal approvals. Separately, the Lesotho Court of Appeal in C of A (CIV) 28/2025, delivered 7 November 2025, dismissed an LHDA appeal and confirmed a High Court order compelling it to pay a second and final tranche of compensation to a society representing the Bobete community in Thaba-Tseka; that case concerns the Phase 1 In-Stream Flow Requirement policy, not Polihali, and is not part of this entry.

dropped.candidate: MICI-PE-2015-0094 Rural Land Titling PTRT-3, Peruvian Amazon
dropped.reason: Fails test 2, and the drop is confirmed on an independent read. I downloaded the MICI Compliance Review Report for PTRT-3 (PE-L1026, loan 3370/OC-PE) from https://www.iadb.org/document.cfm?id=EZIDB0000559-1009163277-2745 and extracted 4,349 lines of text. I read the determination paragraphs 2.148, 2.152, 2.156, 2.160 and 2.163 and the whole 'Harm' block of the conclusions, and searched the full text for 'displaced', 'lost their land', 'invasion', 'evict', 'killed', 'death' and 'threat'. Every harm heading in the conclusions is hedged: 'Potential harm related to shortcomings in the consultation processes' ('may have made it impossible', 'could have prevented'); 'Potential harm related to inadequate categorization' ('may have played a role'); and 'Harm related to the inadequate identification of socioenvironmental risks' ('may have intensified the vulnerability of the lands, environment, health, and culture'). The only unhedged consequence is under 'Potential harm related to failure to meet targets for titling Native communities': the failure to meet titling targets 'led to frustration, disillusionment, and a sense of having been deceived', 'causing to maintain the legal insecurity of tenure over their territories' and undermining confidence in the IDB. That is a benefit not delivered and a pre-existing insecurity left in place, not land, income, health, liberty or life lost. The violence the report does describe - at least 15 Indigenous leaders murdered in Peru's Amazon since 2013, and threats and assassination attempts against AIDESEP - is in section 1.5, 'Context of violence in the Peruvian Amazon', and is attributed to illegal loggers, miners and illicit crops; Management's own comment on the draft report says that section sets out the geographic and social context. The two deaths at line 762 are from the 2020 political crisis, sourced to Human Rights Watch, and are not project-related. Nothing in the report records project-caused harm that happened.

Nothing was found that adds a new co-lender, co-financier or investor, so this is a drop and not an extend.

dropped.candidate: IRM RQ 2010/2 Medupi coal plant, Lephalale
dropped.reason: Cut on test 2: nothing in the documents records harm that happened. I opened the IRM Compliance Review of 19 December 2011 (https://aconsole-static.s3.amazonaws.com/media/public/cases/CR_Report.pdf, 2,446 lines of text) and the fifth monitoring report of 28 January 2022 (https://aconsole-static.s3.amazonaws.com/media/public/cases/medupi_monitor_5.pdf, 747 lines), and read the Water Access, Land and Water Degradation, Consultation and Issues of Graves sections in full. (1) The land and water finding is a hedge, not a finding of damage: 'It is important to note that the evidence of water and land degradation, if it occurs, will not be clear until the power plant is operational. Consequently, it is not possible to reach a firm conclusion about Bank compliance with the applicable policies before Medupi becomes operational.' The whole discussion is of risk - the ash dump 'could leach', 'there may be greater risk from particulate matter', 'the community is anxious' - and the IRM says the validity of the air-quality concern 'is difficult to evaluate in the absence of a strong research base'. (2) The sand mining strand does not carry the case. The compliance report mentions the Mokolo River only as the Requestors' allegation of 'allegedly unlawful sand dredging'. The phrase 'damage done to Mokolo River' that the draft was built on appears only in the IRM Second Monitoring Findings column of the monitoring table, in a sentence whose claim is procedural: an environmental assessment done for a sand mining licence application 'could not substitute for an independent assessment of the damage done to Mokolo River and the rehabilitation requirements by previous legal and illegal sand mining operations'. The damage needing assessment is attributed there to previous legal and illegal sand mining, not to the Medupi works, and the Fourth Monitoring Findings record that the Department of Mineral Resources handled and closed the matter, concluding that Eskom 'could not be responsible for the rehabilitation of all mined areas'. The action is marked completed. (3) The monitoring report's own water finding runs the other way, and the draft omitted it: at action 3.3 the IRM's second and third monitoring findings both say 'Water quality appears not to have been affected by the construction of the Medupi Plant. Water quality is being adequately monitored by Eskom.' (4) The graves finding is a finding about the Bank and about risk, not a record of desecration: the Panel finds the Bank 'was not sufficiently rigorous in its assessment of this policy to determine either that no graves had been or could have been desecrated by the Medupi project or that the borrower had established adequate procedures to consult'. No grave is recorded as desecrated. Management's position is confirmed as drafted - two graves on the site, one an old grave with an affidavit showing it had not been visited since 1967, which Eskom relocated to a formal cemetery following the appropriate legal procedures, and the grave of a child whose mother had agreed in principle but was being prevented from signing - and the fifth monitoring report records remediation: a heritage assessment, graves identified on the Medupi site, cleansing and appeasement ceremonies, and a memorial site. Remediation is not harm. The single relocation in the compliance report is the one full-time worker on one of the purchased farms, 'relocated, with his consent, by the owner of this farm to one of his other properties' - consented, and done by the farm owner. (5) The emissions figures are accurate but document non-compliance with licence limits, not harm, and the draft said so itself. I opened Eskom's annual emissions report for April 2025 to March 2026 and confirmed every figure: 12 SO2 exceedances of the 3,500 mg/Nm3 monthly limit, all at Unit 4 in February 2026 and 'All the exceedances were due to the faulty CEMS'; 40 PM exceedances of the 50 mg/Nm3 daily limit, of which 22 were within start-up and shutdown grace, 12 were due to faulty CEMS and 6 were reported as section 30 incidents; 12 NOx readings above 750 mg/Nm3, also 'due to faulty CEMS'; and on ambient air, 'There were no exceedances of the PM10 daily limit, the SO2 daily limit and the NO2 hourly limit recorded during 2025 monitoring period', with the area non-compliant only on ozone, which Eskom attributes to multiple sources including neighbouring third parties. Of 20 dust fall-out buckets, 18 recorded no exceedances; D15a exceeded the 1,200 mg/m2/day non-residential limit 6 times, peaking at 4,645 in October 2025, and D5a 3 times, peaking at 3,979. (6) That report also fails test 3 independently. It covers 2025-26, and the IRM's fifth monitoring report says the project 'has already been fully disbursed and therefore, there is little leverage on the part the Bank to influence the borrower', and that the IRM decided 'to suspend the annual monitoring until at least 2026'. The AfDB money was gone and the Bank no longer supervised when those readings were taken. Because the case is cut, the draft's 'wb' lender key was not pursued; the World Bank's US$3.75 billion Eskom Investment Support Project loan and Inspection Panel case 65 were not verified against a World Bank document during this check. There is no existing Medupi case in cases.json, so this is a drop, not a duplicate. If the owner wants a Medupi case later, the thing to look for is a document that records harm having occurred - a health study, a court finding, or a water or soil result - because the IRM and the Inspection Panel both stopped at risk.
